sections.markdown:
**Think of Riverpod as a global smart cache with automatic garbage collection.**

`provider` was a note board attached to the widget tree — you had to *hang it* somewhere and children below could read. Riverpod moves the note board out of the widget tree entirely: providers live in a **`ProviderContainer`** (mounted at root via `ProviderScope`). Any widget (or another provider, or a plain Dart function) can call `ref.watch(myProvider)` and get the current value.

- **`ref.watch(p)`** — subscribes; the current widget rebuilds (or the current provider recomputes) on change.
- **`ref.read(p)`** — one-shot, no subscription. Callbacks + `initState`.
- **`ref.listen(p, cb)`** — side effects on state change (nav, snackbar).
- **`family`** — parameterized providers: `userProvider(42)` — one provider instance per argument.
- **`autoDispose`** — provider deletes itself when no widget is watching. Perfect for screen-scoped data.
- **Compile-time DI** — no more `ProviderNotFoundException` at runtime; the framework knows about every provider at compile time (with `riverpod_generator`).

**Why Riverpod became the new default for new Flutter apps:** it fixes provider's runtime-safety hole (missing scope = crash), removes `BuildContext` dependency (test providers in pure Dart, use them from Dart services / isolates), and gives a beautiful `AsyncValue<T>` type for async state (loading / data / error) that eliminates boilerplate boolean flags. Same author (Remi Rousselet). It's provider v2 with lessons learned.

**Riverpod** (`flutter_riverpod`, `riverpod`, `riverpod_annotation` + `riverpod_generator`) is a compile-safe, BuildContext-free, cache-based state-management library. **Provider types:** `Provider` (immutable), `StateProvider` (mutable value), `StateNotifierProvider` (mutable notifier — deprecated in favor of Notifier), `NotifierProvider` (v2), `FutureProvider` / `AsyncNotifierProvider` (async data), `StreamProvider`. **Modifiers:** `.family` (parameterized), `.autoDispose` (GC when unused). **Access:** `ref.watch / read / listen`. Runs providers in pure Dart — no widget tree required for tests.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Forgetting `ProviderScope` at the root.** Nothing watches, providers never build, silent breakage. Wrap `runApp(ProviderScope(child: MyApp()))`.
**Mistake 2: `ref.watch` in a callback (`onPressed`).** Only allowed in `build` / provider bodies. Use `ref.read` in callbacks.
**Mistake 3: Missing `autoDispose` on screen-scoped async data.** Provider caches forever → stale search results linger. Add `.autoDispose` or `@riverpod` (defaults to autoDispose).
**Mistake 4: Not cancelling in `ref.onDispose`.** When a screen leaves + autoDispose kicks in, in-flight requests keep running. Register cancel in `ref.onDispose`.
**Mistake 5: `ref.watch` on a family with a mutable argument.** New search string → new provider instance every keystroke. Debounce upstream or memoize the arg.
**Mistake 6: Mixing legacy StateNotifier + new NotifierProvider.** Code splits between styles. Migrate to `Notifier` / `AsyncNotifier` (v2 API).
**Mistake 7: Ignoring `AsyncValue.guard`.** Manual `try/catch` around emits leaves state in inconsistent AsyncLoading. Use `state = await AsyncValue.guard(() async { ... })`.
**Mistake 8: Testing via widgets when a `ProviderContainer` works.** `container.read(provider)` in pure Dart is faster + more focused.
## Best practices
**1. Use `riverpod_generator` (`@riverpod`)** — codegen removes boilerplate + adds compile-time safety.
**2. `AsyncValue.when` / switch — never manual loading flags.**
**3. `autoDispose` for screen-scoped data;** `keepAlive: true` for long-lived DI (Repository, ApiClient).
**4. `family` for parameterized providers** — `userProvider(id)`.
**5. Cancel + free on `ref.onDispose`.**
**6. `ref.listen` for side effects.**
**7. Compose via `ref.watch(otherProvider)` inside providers** — derived state.
**8. Test with `ProviderContainer` in pure Dart** — no widget tree.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Counter with `@riverpod class Counter extends _$Counter`; use `ref.watch` in build.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — `FutureProvider` + `AsyncValue.when` for a user profile.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — `family` + `autoDispose` — `feedProvider(query: q)`.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — `ref.onDispose` cancels an in-flight Dio request when the screen pops.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — Compose two async providers (user + settings) into a derived AsyncValue.
**Practice 6 (Expert)** — `ProviderContainer` test that overrides an ApiClient with a fake + asserts state transitions.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: What does Riverpod fix from `provider`?**

**A:** **(1) Compile-time DI safety.** In `provider`, forgetting to wrap a widget = runtime `ProviderNotFoundException`. Riverpod's providers are global (not tree-scoped), and with `riverpod_generator` the compiler knows every provider; a missing dep is a compile error. **(2) No `BuildContext` dependency.** `ref.watch(p)` works from providers and pure Dart, so you can compose providers, test them without widgets, and use them from services / isolates. **(3) `AsyncValue<T>`.** Single sealed type for loading / data / error — no boolean-flag soup. **(4) `family` + `autoDispose`.** First-class parameterized + garbage-collected providers. **(5) Reactive composition.** `ref.watch(otherProvider)` inside a provider builds derived state automatically. **Same author** as `provider`; Riverpod is essentially provider v2 with hard-earned lessons. **Cost:** small learning curve; codegen build step.

**Q2: Explain `.family` and `.autoDispose` and when to use each.**

**A:** **`.family`** — parameterized providers. Instead of one global `userProvider`, you write `userProvider.family` (or use `@riverpod Future<User> user(UserRef ref, int id)` with the generator). Each unique argument instantiates a separate provider instance, cached by (provider × arg). Use for per-entity data: `userProvider(42)`, `productProvider(sku)`. **`.autoDispose`** — provider deletes itself when nothing watches. Perfect for screen-scoped data (search results, transient forms) that should NOT survive the user leaving the screen. Combine: `feedProvider.family.autoDispose` — one instance per query, gone when the search bar clears. **Trap:** with `.family`, mutable arguments (a search string that changes per keystroke) creates a new provider every keystroke; combine with debounce. **`keepAlive: true`** — the escape hatch to keep an autoDispose provider alive after unwatch (e.g., preload for next screen).

**Q3: How does `AsyncValue<T>` simplify async state?**

**A:** `AsyncValue<T>` is a sealed type: `AsyncData(value)`, `AsyncLoading()`, `AsyncError(err, st)`. Pattern-match in UI via `.when(data: ..., loading: ..., error: ...)`. **Composition wins:** `ref.watch(providerA.future)` inside `providerB` propagates loading/error automatically — you don't juggle three booleans. **Mutation:** `state = const AsyncLoading()` then `state = await AsyncValue.guard(() async { ... })` — guard converts thrown exceptions to `AsyncError` cleanly. **Refresh:** `ref.invalidate(provider)` triggers rebuild; `ref.refresh(provider)` returns the new future. **Comparison to `flutter_bloc`:** Bloc requires you to model `Loading / Data / Error` states manually via sealed classes; AsyncValue gives it for free. **Trap:** don't ignore `AsyncError` — always show at least a snackbar. `.whenData` skips loading/error paths silently which can hide bugs.

**Q4: How do you test Riverpod providers?**

**A:** **`ProviderContainer`** — pure Dart, no widget tree. Construct one, optionally override providers (`overrides: [apiProvider.overrideWithValue(FakeApi())]`), then `container.read(myProvider)` to trigger + assert. **`container.listen(myProvider, cb)`** — subscribe + capture state transitions. **`container.dispose()`** — teardown. **Async testing:** `await container.read(userProvider.future)` waits for the FutureProvider to settle. **Test AsyncValue transitions** — expect `AsyncLoading → AsyncData` or `AsyncLoading → AsyncError`. **Widget tests:** wrap SUT in `ProviderScope(overrides: [...])` for integration checks. **Also:** `riverpod_lint` catches common mistakes (missing autoDispose, ref.watch in callback) statically. **Interview highlight:** 'no BuildContext required for provider tests' — this is the tangible win over provider / flutter_bloc.

**Q5: How would you cancel an in-flight request when the user leaves a screen?**

**A:** Combine `autoDispose` + `ref.onDispose` + Dio's `CancelToken`. Inside the provider: `final cancel = CancelToken(); ref.onDispose(cancel.cancel); return repo.load(cancel: cancel);`. When the widget stops watching (screen pop, argument change), Riverpod disposes the provider → `ref.onDispose` fires → CancelToken cancels → Dio throws DioException(cancel) → your repo swallows or propagates. **Advantages** over provider's manual dispose: automatic, screen-scoped, no `BuildContext` needed, works for `family` too (each family instance disposed independently). **Also:** `ref.keepAlive()` can be called + released later — useful for preloading; when released, autoDispose kicks in on next unwatch. **Common bug:** forgetting `.autoDispose` — provider caches forever, cancel never fires. `riverpod_generator` defaults to autoDispose which is safer.

**Q6: Riverpod vs flutter_bloc vs provider — pick one for a new app and defend.**

**A:** **New app, small-to-mid team, no historic constraints → Riverpod.** Compile-time safety, AsyncValue, ergonomic composition, minimal boilerplate with codegen. **Existing large team with `flutter_bloc` muscle memory → keep flutter_bloc.** Migration cost is high; the architectural benefits are equivalent. **Prototype / learning / very small app → `provider`.** Least learning curve; official Flutter tutorial. **Regulated audit-log requirements → `flutter_bloc`** (explicit event stream is a compliance win). **Wrong answer at interview:** 'Riverpod is objectively best' — nuance matters. **The real signal:** knowing when to STAY on your current stack vs migrate. Migration for its own sake is expensive; migrate only when you're hitting real pain (runtime provider errors, unmaintainable derived state, difficult tests).

## Real-world usage

- **Default for new Flutter apps in 2025-2026** — most YouTube tutorials, indie apps, mid-sized startups.
- **Composition-heavy screens** — dashboards combining N async sources.
- **Screen-scoped async with cancel-on-leave** — feed, search, chat.
- **NOT ideal for** — teams with heavy investment in flutter_bloc / MobX; churn > gain.

## Advanced notes

- **`riverpod_generator`** — annotations + codegen; strongly recommended in 2.x.
- **`riverpod_lint`** — static analysis catching common mistakes.
- **`ref.invalidate` / `ref.refresh`** — trigger rebuild.
- **`ProviderObserver`** — global hook for `didAddProvider`, `didUpdateProvider`, `didDisposeProvider`. Wire to Crashlytics.
- **`ProviderScope` overrides** — inject fakes at test time or feature-flag stages.
- **`ref.watch(p.select((v) => v.slice))`** — analog to provider's `Selector`; narrow rebuild scope.
- **`ref.keepAlive()` in provider body** — protect from autoDispose until `link.close()`.
- **`Family` args must have stable equality** — use `Equatable` or freezed value classes for complex args.
- **`AsyncValue.guard`** — turns thrown exceptions into AsyncError.
- **`unmounted` guard** — inside a Notifier, check `ref.mounted` before mutating state after an async gap.
- **Dependency graph** — Riverpod builds a DAG; cycles throw; `ref.watch` cycles are rare in practice.
- **Companion**: `hooks_riverpod` adds `flutter_hooks` — `useState`, `useEffect` in Flutter. Popular in Riverpod-heavy codebases.
